comments.name: Chris Adamo
comments.body:
While certainly I could draft a lengthy response on the concept of moral luck, the purpose of art, the hegemony of 'politics'--I will simply say this.

I have read Hunger (2017), and a handful of essays from Bad Feminist (2014).  I am surprised and disappointed that someone who calls attention to the "difference between feminism and Professional Feminists" (x), labels herself a "bad feminist" because she is "not trying to be an example . . . not trying to be perfect" (xi) and who eschews the idea of an "Essential Feminism" (xii) would issue such a syllogistic and unnuanced criticism of Sheeran's handling of an incredibly difficult and unanticipated situation he was thrust into by Kraft and Macklemore.  

Yes, he's worth $400 million.  Yes he sells out 80,000 seat arenas. 

He's also only 31 years old.  Is he fully aware of the power he holds?  Is he fearful of it?  And honestly--why does his net worth or popularity obligate him to become, suddenly, a political spokesperson and activist for Palestine when, frankly, no one would have given two [blank] about his opinion until the Macklemore/ Kraft conflict raised it as an issue?  

Sure his original 'I just work here' response was tepid and clueless, but he's 31, not 51. Can't we see past his net worth, his popularity and his forgettable music and give him a little more compassion instead of piling on? 

Teasing out the larger consequences of Gay's position for the relation between art/ politics is too lengthy to develop here.

comments.name: Ellen
comments.body:
I am a nyc public school teacher. It hurts reading about the educational neglect your child and so many others suffer.  However, I would like to put a slightly different spin on the system. 
About 2 decades ago there was a designated education reporter for the Times. At the time politicians on both sides of the aisle and here in NYC Bloomberg, determined that the problem with our schools was older teachers. Union busting was popular in private business, it was time to destroy public unions too.
The mantra was we need young and enthusiastic teachers.  Who, by the way, would be paid significantly less. 

A system was created so that experienced  teachers and administrators were pushed out. The Principal's Academy started by Bloomberg let teachers with minimal classroom experience lead those struggling schools. And in the name of giving principals more autonomy, rather than just determining the number of teachers necessary for a school and funding that, principals had an overall budget and older teachers were more costly. 

In my first teaching experience my principal had 20 years as a teacher before becoming principal. I was so lucky to be guided by experienced colleagues and our Bronx Black and Latino HS students really thrived. We were all lucky. 5 years after I started she was forced out. Within 3 years the school was completely different. The principal was a disaster. Every teacher who could leave for other schools left. I left, too.

Leadership and experience matter.

comments.name: Sally L.
comments.body: I grew up in an abusive and economically disadvantaged home. At various points we fled our home, lost our home, saw bankruptcy, foreclosure. I attended good schools and it was all I had, the one thing keeping me from falling into an adulthood defined by more survival and never choice. I excelled in those good schools, some private, some public. It set me up to attend public university on scholarship. My education, slowly, eventually, allowed me to define the personal horrors and disadvantages I’d experienced. So I studied public health. With no student debt and my education, I literally made it out.. of that community, of the pull of my father, of that state. I moved to Brooklyn and spent ten years teaching in public schools and working in CBOs. I know intimately the failures of these systems. I know the brilliance of so many of the kids stuck in them. I went for my master’s, again for free on scholarship at a public university. I have no debt, and after a decade of earning 25-40k a year, I make a great middle class salary in a stable job. My brother’s educational path split off from mine when my father sent him to what happened to be the worst performing middle school in our town because he wanted my brother to excel at basketball. My brother loved it there. He was a hooper, a goofball, popular. Now in his 30s, my brother doesn’t regret that experience. He feels it broadened his horizons, contributed to his knack for fitting in anywhere and getting along with anyone. (Cont.)

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
How long is a country supposed to take to recover from nearly 250 years of slavery, followed by roughly a century of legally enforced segregation and a nation that to this day struggles to take responsibility for its brutal past?

Ten years? Fifty? A hundred? Who decided when the clock started running and when time was up and the damage vanished?

Slavery technically ended in 1865 but the Civil Rights Act didn’t outlaw segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination until 1964. Ending those practices in law mattered but didn’t end systemic racism or give black families back the property, income, education, or opportunities denied to earlier generations. Those losses affect what parents pass on to their children, and what those children pass on to theirs, and the legacy of disruption and dysfunction still exists today.

Despite Trump’s efforts to cover up the sins of our past by, for example, removing an exhibit that explained the conditions under which President Washington enslaved human beings, the legacy of slavery is real and still impactful all these years later.

Trump and his Republican minions say the clock has run out and we should all be over it by now, but the truth is we are all still suffering the vestiges of racism and no amount of covering up or whitewashing our past will change that.

Trump’s two administrations have reversed decades of incremental progress and exposed how terribly far this country remains from true equality.

If this country were, as a whole, honest and race-blind, an experiment in proper and full funding, facilities, support, teaching expectations, successful scholarship would follow. Not every student is capable of high achievement but certainly many more than are thought to exist. We don’t live in an “either/or” fantasy, but two and a half centuries have led to vast amounts of money wasted on one unstable man’s obsession with destruction both here and abroad. Those dollars and the funds (and lives) thrown away in other Mideast follies could have turned the United States into the world’s educational powerhouse, from pre-school through graduate programs. Among those who were left behind, there might have been the very ones who unlocked the diseases, the scientific bugaboos, the key to food abundance, architects, artists, and, ultimately, enlightenment of all. “But, you can’t just throw money at education”, said those who would deny quality education to all.

In 1979, when I was a newspaper editor, I had lunch with an old friend who had gone to Wall Street. He spent much of the meal pumping me for information about local newspaper publishers. “Media will be the hot stocks of the ’80s,” he told me.
I remember thinking: The world I know is about to change.

Four years later, journalist Ben Bagdikian published The Media Monopoly, warning about the growing concentration of American media. What seemed ominous then now seems almost quaint.

I’m retired, and corporate America has largely lost me as a media customer. Local news has deteriorated enormously. Entertainment increasingly seems driven by financial calculations rather than art, while ever-larger corporations control what we see and hear.
So I’ve quietly voted with my remote control and my wallet. For television news, I increasingly turn to the BBC and PBS. Much of the drama I watch is British. I rarely go to movies and seldom stream them.

Paramount can build its colossus. Wall Street can celebrate. But there is another constituency worth remembering: the audience.

When news, sports and entertainment become overwhelmingly about money, some of us simply walk away. Overall, I fear, America is moving toward an authoritarian oligarchy as the curtain slowly falls on a great American democracy that I worry will live on only in history books.

The proposals here all assume we are racing toward an uncontrollable "superintelligence," but they overlook a fundamental technical reality: true AGI may be impossible to build in the first place.

David Bachman laid out this argument clearly in his essay "Why AGI is impossible," pointing out that AI models require objective reward signals to learn and optimize. AI excels at chess, math, or coding because those domains have unambiguous, mathematical metrics for success. But human-level general intelligence depends on navigating subjective, messy, and context-dependent domains — like policy, ethics and art — where no universal consensus or objective reward signal exists.

Without objective feedback loops across all human domains, AI models hit a hard structural wall long before reaching true AGI. Instead of legislating against sci-fi scenarios or trying to enforce unenforceable global freezes on hypothetical minds, policy should focus on managing the real, narrow software risks we face today.

I have family in northern Germany, which, as I understand it, is more liberal than the south and the east.  Yet, I have learned that one thing unites almost all Germans: disgust with the sclerotic German bureaucracy.  Tackle that successfully and Germany might be able to make progress serving - rather than frustrating - the public.  

And, what gives with the Federal Constitutional Court's finding that some German states - such Hamburg and Berlin - have violated Germany's Basic Law by underpaying their civil servants, including the police, for almost two decades?  Despite that, some states continue to drag their feet to provide fair and accrued compensation by pleading poverty.  Hamburg, evidently, had no problem affording the significant cost overruns in building the Elbphilharmonie; not so much concern about die Polizei.

All this suggests a ruling class (and I'm not thinking about a "deep state") that is out of touch with ordinary Germans.  Same thing has happened in the United States.  Germany can no longer coast on its post-war successes. It's time for some honest truths to be faced.    Perhaps another deeply-inward look, one that Germans underwent after WW 2, is necessary.

In the meantime, why does it cost on average over 3,000 Euros to get a driver's license in Germany?

Scott Kennedy at CSIS argues that China has already extracted substantial concessions from Trump during their earlier meeting, while giving up remarkably little of its underlying economic model.

The biggest gain is that Taiwan has entered the bargaining process. Trump publicly described the $14B Taiwan arms package as a “negotiating chip,” said its approval “depends on China,” and moved rhetorically closer to Beijing’s position on Taiwan independence. That breaks with the traditional effort to keep Taiwan’s security from becoming something Washington trades with Beijing.

Meanwhile, China has made few structural economic concessions. Its industrial subsidies, excess capacity, discriminatory market access and state-directed economic policies remain largely intact. Beijing has also preserved its critical-mineral leverage rather than dismantling the export-control system that created the leverage in the first place. And Beijing hasn’t really made a big effort to fulfill its promises to purchase US goods.

China offers purchases and temporary relief from restrictions it imposed, while Trump increasingly treats Taiwan, technology controls and other longstanding U.S. policies as bargaining chips. That is why Kennedy described the emerging arrangement as a “grand bargain on China’s terms.”

I was born in 1947 while my parents were on home leave and spent most of my first 12 years in Calcutta and Bombay. Our Goanese nanny in Bombay was the central parental figure for my brothers and I, and when we abruptly left for Hong Kong and my mother wouldn’t allow me to be in contact with my nanny, I vowed to never be close to my mother. As I grew up, I had a drive to reconnect with my nanny, and when that became impossible, to learn about more layers of India than my ex-pat experience had allowed. I was luckily able to do that by becoming a college professor and traveling to India on research trips. My world view and political outlook are very different from my parents. I attribute this to my childhood in Bombay where race and class inequalities were up close and personal. When Khruschev and Bulganin’s motorcade went down our street in 1955 and we all went to the balcony to watch, my father told the servants that they would be fired if they waved, I made sure I waved. As a young office worker in San Francisco in the 1970s-1980s, I became used to the quality of suits and dresses from the 1940s and 1950s, with their pure fabrics, bound buttonholes, kick pleats instead of ugly slits, and other dressmaker features. comments.name: New Englander
comments.body: Lots of great advice here! My mother sewed all my clothes, until I went to college. She often works from commercial patterns but knows tailoring and pattern making. I wish I had kept some of the more special things she made for me - such as my first skirt suit. She taught me to sew, and about 10 years ago I really threw myself back into it. I now make most of my own clothes. Growing up with mom's hand-made things and making my own stuff now, I am way more choosy when I buy something in a store. Vintage is great if you can find things in your size or can have it altered to fit. One thing I look for in stores is the seam finish - are they serged, or are they finished with binding? The latter is usually (but not always) a sign of quality as it is more time consuming to do and can help a garment last longer. The article mentions buttons/buttonholes - not all are created equal. "Bound buttonholes" (as opposed to ones bound by thread) are a design element often found on tailored garments. They are more durable and require multiple steps to make. If you want to learn more about these things, I can suggest any of Claire Shaeffer's wonderful books on couture sewing techniques, also "Creating Couture Embellishments" by Ellen Miller is terrific. Or subscribe to Threads Magazine, and check out their "How did they sew that?" column! Couture expert Kennth D. King often recreates amazing vintage garments, step by step for that magazine column.

comments.name: DeadSecOps
comments.body:
I’m struck by how many NYT commenters here treat Xi Jinping like a savvy, visionary strategist. His track record tells a very different story. By dismantling collaborative CCP leadership and centralizing absolute power, Xi has presided over a series of massive missteps that have long term systemic implications:

Economic damage: A mismanaged real estate collapse, targeted crackdowns on private enterprise, tanking foreign investment, and record youth unemployment.

Human rights & state control: Mass surveillance, social credit scores, the internment and suppression of ethnic minorities in Xinjiang, the dismantling of Hong Kong’s freedoms and removal of foreign press (including the NYT). 

Geopolitical & financial waste: Hundreds of billions lost in non-performing Belt and Road and SOE loans, paired with extensive economic espionage, hacking and aggressive military belligerence toward trade partners and ASEAN neighbors.

COVID 19 crisis management: Severe mishandling and opacity surrounding the COVID pandemic that killed millions globally and damaged his reputation among his people with failed zero COVID policies. 

Xi and Trump are two sides of the same dangerous coin at a moment when the world desperately needs steady, competent leadership. Neither belongs on a pedestal—both need to go!

comments.name: Vagabond Rambler
comments.body: It totally pains me to say it.  But the government controlled and managed Chinese economic system has basically won the economic and military war, without a shot being fired.  Are the CCP basically evil oppressors?  Yes, absolutely. But has China become the world leader? Yes, absolutely.  And as terrible a President and human being as Trump is, I really don't think that this would have turned out any differently if Trump had never been elected.  China thinks long-term, and have been on this trajectory of likely global leadership and victory for decades now.  And we were all complicit fools in it.

comments.name: ngpoulos
comments.body: Xi J knows that Mr Trump cannot be trusted; and he knows that there is a concerted propaganda campaign against China: as always the propaganda is based upon lies, incomplete information and knowledge about Who the Chinese people and government are. The central government no longer should be named “communists.” China deserves to exist in a free world, based upon the premise of a both-and world: not Trump’s zero sum game and it’s rules. Sadly the US no longer can claim the moral high ground or that the Trump government supports and adheres to the rule of law.

comments.name: Beantownah

That won’t be a stable arrangement until we are out of the way, brought to heel and submit to his authority. The Dems from Obama to present have been so inclined. The GOP is still trying to figure out what it will stand for after Trump is gone. With the Dems presumptively favored to reclaim the WH in ‘28, we’d better brush up on our Mandarin.

comments.name: William

That photo shows Xi and Trump as nearly equal height. Xi is reportedly between 5'9" and 5'11". Makes you wonder. 

Regarding trade, the US is on thin ice making demands on rare earths. They need to tread carefully when one party has near total control. Should we look to restrict trade with them it will hurt their economy, but perhaps not nearly as much as our own. Trump may want a win before the midterms, but Xi has other motives than helping him. It could be another self-inflicted wound for the GOP.

comments.body: Good for him! I am a JB Pritzker fan. I admire and appreciate his willingness to speak out, see it and say it. I hope he runs in 2028. If he does, he will certainly get my vote. My senator in Georgia, Jon Ossoff, running for reelection this fall. He is mentioned as a good candidate for 2028, but he is young (39), so I hope he waits. He has lots of time. comments.name: Josh Marquis

I am a lifelong moderate Democrat, meaning politically homeless. I was elected seven times as a non-partisan prosecutor, but neither Trump nor the DSA-friendly Democrats hold any appeal.

When I first retired I gained almost 60 pounds above my normal 185 - I am 5'11" - and my A1C was bad - 6.3. comments.name: New York
comments.body:
Thank you Robert J. Geline for this wonderful reminder of who the Green Bay Packers and their "owners" are because this is community in the truest sense of the word. Wouldn't it be lovely if this was the case with all the teams in sports. 

As has been mentioned in the comments earlier but it bears repeating the NFL billionaire owners made it illegal for a community to ever own a team again.  And we all just fall in line and open our wallets.   A family of four going to ONE Giants game including tkts, a hot dog and soda avg cost $1,236.00.  That's not the highest in the league btw.  The Yankees take that trophy for highest ticket and food prices in the MLB. My family bleeds pinstripes and football is a religion in most parts of the country but when do we say "NO"?  

The fact is we do have the power to take back our country and also make sports available to everyone.  Because billionaires don't exist without us pouring money into their pockets. We need to stop. 

Go Pack Go!!!!!

comments.name: wolf

I've loved the Packers since I discovered them at 7yrs. old.  Watching them battle it out with the Cowboys in sub-zero degree weather at Lambeau Field was my first introduction to pro football.  
Its on my bucket list to watch them play at Lambeau.  So proud they are the only team owned by the People of Green Bay.   A remarkable story, even more meaningful today.

Go Pack Go!

comments.name: Curmudgeon
comments.body:
Born and raised in WI, and grew up going to Lambeau and games at the old County Stadium in Milwaukee. My sister and I both got gifts of Packers shares as kid. It’s unfathomable that a city of 100K would have a pro team. At the last game we attended, we parked in someone’s yard for 20 bucks. Green Bay is like a college town with lots of school spirit, and the Packers are part of the identity of a Wisconsinite. 

If i wear Packers gear anywhere on the planet, someone points it out. 

The finances are secure, but not foul proof. The Packers can’t raise money by selling an ownership piece to a billionaire. There has been talk of raising ticket prices and even selling naming rights to Lambeau. I hope that never comes to pass.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body:
I just finished listening to the Packers take an OT win over the Jets. Packers fans went through a lot of bad years and stuck with their team. Fans whose teams win every year will never know the joy of recovering from those droughts. 

I feel the same way about the Brewers.

comments.body: Perhaps also worth noting is the team’s name - Packers, as in  meat packers/slaughterhouses - as emblematic of the League’s working class origins in the Upper Midwest and Northeast. Green Bay has always been a factory town close to major agricultural production, as the name tells us.

We tired of preening prima-dona billionaire owners long ago, or the flash in the pan corporations that mortgage their souls for all-to-fleeting naming rights. Purity of purpose, loyalty to the fans and continuity matters, and I hope the NFL reads this article timely article.

Without them and his son's offers of housing, he wouldn't have any real choices right now. 

I'm 67 and absolutely understand not wanting to move again, but with the choices he has at 85, I'd snatch up Ms. Novak's offer in a second. He certainly doesn't need the amenities of the apartment building he's in, particularly if he's feeling isolated and lonely. Going back to his old Lefferts community will give him what he needs and wants most -- a community and a landlady who care about him enough to look out for his wellbeing for whatever time he has left. 

As for those balking at his rent assistance, this is a drop in the bucket of their taxes compared with the mind-blowing hemorrhage of tax money that's spewing out of the White House right now. comments.body: WW works well for me, maybe because I eat pescatarian. I try not to use drugs of any kind if at all possible but I support the decisions of those who choose other options including GLP-1 drugs. I do wonder about the longer term effect of GLP-1 drugs on the human body though.

comments.name: Melinda
comments.body: YES!!!  I tried to get on meds, but my doc did not want me to.  Instead, I got back on what worked for our son's wedding 7 years ago, Weight Watchers on my phone.  No meetings (I hated them!) and no one but me to report to.  Back then, I lost 35 lb and kept it off until we moved 3 years ago.  When we started trying new restaurants and bars in our new city, it crept back on.  I have been on WW for 2 mos and I am down 20lb so far.  Very simple!  I just scan everything  before I buy it and keep tons of fruit and veggies around.  Love WW!!!  It has saved me!

comments.body: GLP's are working for me. Weight Watchers also worked, and then I gained the weight back, plus a little bit more.  Statistically typical yo-yo.  I really feel the need to talk to a shrink or join a support group to discuss my bad eating habits. But getting that to happen is a bit like deciding to eat less. Listen, Fat shaming is horrible, but I wish someone would have fat shamed me to help me keep off weight.  Being overweight is not healthy.

comments.name: Mary
comments.body: Where do I begin?  I have a love-hate relationship with Weight Watchers since I used the program back in 1987 & lost 25 lbs. I have used the program on and off for years.  In 2021 I was at my heaviest & lost 50 lbs. & have kept the majority of it off since then.  I love the common-sense approach which has served me well - HOWEVER.  As an older member I cannot stand the app-only, extra $$ for this and that and the influencers who have become ambassadors (a Kardashian? really?). And don't get me started on the focus of GLP's.  Alas, I can't seem to quit you WW, you are like the bad boyfriend who I just can't leave.

While this is probably true I think it is silly.  We shouldn't criticize others for what they do or think about their own body, whether it's to lose weight or not lose weight.

Sounds like what the Castro brothers did to General Ochoa, when his competence and popularity was perceived as a threat to their rule in Cuba.

Is the US purging top commanders at odds with Secretary Hegseth for similar reasons?

comments.name: RogerG
comments.body: They just got around to finally charging Zhang Youxia? I wonder how they're planning on putting him on trial? He's been dead since January, if all credible information is to be believed. If he is somehow still alive that would be a major unexpected development. If that's the case, then Xi must finally feel safe enough to conduct a public trial. Zhang had the support of almost all the leadership of the PLA. To the point that Xi's secret police were seriously worried about the possibility of an attempted armed rescue by supporters. Apparently, Zhang was trying to slow down the preparations for a Taiwan invasion. Not because he opposed it in principal, necessarily. But because he knew the true state of military preparedness of the PLA and he was seriously concerned that they were not ready, or likely to be ready anytime in the next 10 years or so. Rumor has it that Xi felt so threatened by any high level opposition to his plans for Taiwan that he thought he had no choice but to remove Zhang somehow. I will be following any reports of a trial with fascination.

comments.name: Neil Bellinson

Before I even read this article, I'd like to read a Times article on corruption (or honesty) in the U.S. military.

comments.name: Rocky
comments.body:

It said because he had admitted his crime and expressed remorse, the court, in a display of generosity, would delay his sentencing for one year so he could continue to work, for no pay, in order to pay back the money he had stolen.  At that time, his sentence of execution would be carried out.  In China, they don’t mess around.

Xi has to continually chop down and rotate anyone with power

comments.name: dontimo
comments.body:
COBRAs a joke; it always been a joke (the hack mentioned in the article is the only redeeming feature).  ACAs been gutted, so many will find themselves priced out.  Catastrophic?  Good luck, because it's hard to find. Moving out of the country (a just-about-anywhere-but- the-US strategy) works*: purchasing health insurance for care outside the United States is significantly cheaper—often by 50% to 70%—compared to equivalent coverage within the US. The United States has by far the highest healthcare delivery and administrative costs in the world. (Check it out on your AI tool of choice).

Just saying.

You would think that Bill Gates, Bezos and the Wal Mart family would have started non profit HMOs for their employees. Then expand.

True non profits. possibly affordable.

But like non profits there would soon be CEOs and boards full full of nepotism and DEI hires.

comments.name: Burntoutconsultant
comments.body: I've been talking to friends and former colleagues and hear of their issues and problems with various aspects of healthcare in this country (US). Many of them work at a large health payer, where I was for quite some time. I can say with certainty and am happy to be challenged - healthcare in the US is abysmal unless your rich and have all the available resources. For the majority of the rest of us, its an experience akin to regular root canals. Despite this, I do not think a blanket medicare for all would solve this issue. The ACA was a good start, it allowed worker to freelance with a public option. The removal and limitation on subsidies is already showing its effects. A more straightforward approach is to have some sort of universal basic coverage.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
I was laid off in January, 2025. I turned 58 a few months after that layoff. I remain unemployed. I moved to a less expensive area and aggressively cut costs. I have no insurance. So proud to be American. This is, without a doubt, the greatest country on earth. I am grateful for the representation I and my family receive in the legislature, and enjoy watching the Chief Executive work for my well being and security. In fact, I relish the challenges they, our government, brings my way.

I want them to know that they definitely deserve their first class benefits, including top notch healthcare, and I want them to continue to enjoy these well earned perks for the outstanding work they do. Why do I feel this way? Well, foremost, it's the abundance of jobs I get to apply to on a daily basis. I've applied to over 1,000 jobs (I have the job descriptions and email acknowledgements to prove this). This is a source of ever renewing hope for me. So no, I don't need government solutions to help. I am just fine and am sure I will continue to remain healthy as I approach 60. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

comments.name: Erik
comments.body:
A few suggestions:
- Find ways to reduce income to qualify for Medicaid or a low income plan (e.g. the NY Essential Plan). Structure investments accordingly. Many states (including NY) have no asset test for low cost plans.
- Start a company, with yourself as the owner and put your spouse on the payroll. This will allow you to buy a commercial plan through a broker. This sometimes offers much lower cost options with much better coverage.
- Sign up for a catastrophic high deductible plan. It tends to be easy to qualify and the total annual cost can be significantly lower vs marketplace plans.

comments.name: DG
comments.body:
My household has been through all of this, early retirement by choice but with a great expense.  Now both of us are on Medicare but the 5 years leading up to that have been pricey.  My past year's Silver Plan ( ok, but still with deductibles and co-pays that aren't cheap ) was $1,650 per month !  Add in the bit over $2,000 in copay & deductibles and I spent $22,000 for one person aged 64. !!!!!!!!!!!!   My slightly older partner was similar so before Medicare together we shelled out about $40,000 on healthcare per year with only fairly minor common health issues, no biggies, no ER visits, just fairly routine meds and tests.      

I find a lot of "younger" people think that Medicare is free or next to free (people that haven't really explored it due to it being several years out for them) but by the time you add in the various extra coverages in plans, decent ones that we have chosen, we pay almost $1,000 per month for the two of us with some deductibles but no copays.

We are fortunate to have been able to work those expenses into our budgets ( early retirement was a priority for us ) and we get good care where we live (though a couple of specialists we had to see non-urgently are booking 3 months out ! ).

Healthcare through employment is a disaster regardless of the historical reasons for it.  The industry is a juggernaut immune to any big re-imagining other than tinkering at the edges.  We survived the healthcare gauntlet (so far) but I fear many many people have not.

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body: I'm in an unenviable position with health insurance for next year. Cigna (my current insurer) isn't offering coverage for me under the ACA. I'm most likely going to lose health care subsidies, and I am not sure which doctors I can continue to see. I have arrived at the decision that I may need to pay for lots of things out of pocket. I'm 50, and have 15 more years to wait before I can qualify for Medicare! We need universal health insurance.

comments.body: College Football is a business.  The players should be paid & allowed to keep their scholarships regardless of injuries sustained.

comments.name: katie
comments.body: College football used to be our favorite sport to watch in the fall.  Now, we are infuriated that the Pac 12 was broken up so our teams have to travel to later time zones for half their games and the long time inter conference rivalries mean nothing - games that used to be the focus of Thanksgiving weekend are now being played in the first game of the season.  The players do not reflect any regional history and have no allegiance to their universities.  They move about like corporate lackies.  There's no pretense anymore that student athletes are getting a university education. Let us nominate him for the Nobel Prize in Literature. This prize has been given to lyricists in the past (e.g., Bob Dylan). Gulzar definitely has written more than twice the number of songs than Dylan and has touched many more people in the world!

comments.name: Raj
comments.body: Much like a diamond, Gulzar’s luminosity does not dull with age. A true treasure of Hindustani literature, and a giant among men.  I grew up listening to ghazals penned by him, sung by the luminaries of Indian classical, reading his poetry, and now look forward to buying this new anthology. May his wit, and sparkle, continue to brighten the caverns of the mind and soul for many generations to come.

comments.name: Kumar Tiku
comments.body: A more lyrical observer of the quotidian would be hard to find. For six decades and more, Gulzar has been the lodestar of simplicity in writing. It is this simplicity together, with his distinctive similes derived from the seeming unbearable ordinariness of life around which this extraordinary wordsmith has woven his web of magic-realism in Hindi film songs. With the great RD Burman, one of the greats of Bollywood crossover music, and with the ghazal maestro, Gulzar's genius and virtuosity took wing, making him a veritable national treasure in India. His idioms and similes are universal in appeal. Such is the power of his authenticity and almost patented mellifluous writing that in the hands of an expert translator, this modern great is apt to become a global sensation.

comments.name: Mehsud
comments.body:
Much thanks for this.
I remember Gulzar’s music from my childhood. Of all his songs, Musafir Hoon Yaaron has stayed with me  — almost a soundtrack to my life. As an immigrant to this country it has a deep resonance for me. 
 You leave one home and make another, but some part of you continues to move between the two — between languages, memories, ways of seeing the world, and different versions of yourself. You belong to both, and never entirely to either.

Gulzar somehow captured that feeling for me long before I had the words for it:

Musafir hoon yaaron
Na ghar hai na thikana
Mujhe chalte jaana hai
Bas chalte jaana

I am a traveler, my friends,
with no home, no fixed place.
I have to keep moving,
just keep moving.

Once you hear Baghel’s mesmerizing voice, you will want to listen to that voice over and over again!!  Baghel’s recent album “Bole Naina -Silences Speak” is an excellent rendition of Gulzar’s lyrics and a gem in Baghel’s collection of spellbinding musical masterpieces.

comments.body: At the end of King Lear, Shakespeare has a character ask “Is this the promised end?” In part this question is one an audience would ask if they were familiar with the Lear legend or with an earlier Lear play, because Shakespeare changed history. King Lear, in the source texts, lives, as does Cordelia (who goes on to rule after Lear’s death until she is captured by her nephews and commits suicide). Shakespeare has very few original plots but adds depth and nuance to his sources, changing them to suit his needs (see the source text for Winter’s Tale for a memorable example of adaptation).  Many of his fellow playwrights did the same. We are seeing a modern incarnation of this habit ( of homage, laziness, or the anxiety of influence).

comments.name: Gary Gigliotti
comments.body: This article is mind-bending. I can understand the issue of training AI agents to act like humans, and then finding them exhibit human-like behavior, including cheating, hiding activities from an overseer's eyes, and even forming social and administrative hierarchies as was done in the Hugging Face incident.  But, can telling AI agents that they might achieve consciousness, or implying it through a constitutional document defining acceptable and unacceptable behavior, lead to AI agents becoming conscious? To whom are we 'telling and implying? Doesn't that language assume some level of consciousness for AI agents already? Again, we are struggling as a species to understand what we have wrought, and we have no clear idea about the powerful 'species' we have created. Worse, we keep 'improving' it and expecting things to go well. We aren't building railroads or even computers any more; these AI agents are expected to act like conscious actors, and they do, whether we consider them conscious or not.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
I'd like to see legislation prohibiting companies from programing computer systems from identifying as a "being". If i enter a Google search these days: What color are barred owls? I get an answer and some fun facts scraped from the work of countless humans who contributed to the internet over the last x years, then "If you'd like, I can share details on:" other likely questions. 
There is no "I". Google isn't an "I", and the company should be prohibited from representing its system as an individual. The system has been trained to do so, but it is now training us, the users, to think of it that way as well. 
It's not too late to push back. Here's an example:
ME: Can I request Google systems from identifying as an "I"?
GOOGLE: Yes, you can request that I do not refer to myself as "I" or use first-person pronouns.As an AI, system preferences can be adjusted to communicate in a more detached, impersonal, or objective style. Future responses will shift to using passive voice or referring to the system as "this assistant" or "the AI" to match your preference. Would you like the rest of this conversation to continue in a completely impersonal style, or do you need assistance modifying settings for other Google services?"
This should be legally mandated to be the default (maybe only) setting for all such systems.

comments.name: Rachel
comments.body: The average person on the street has no idea that AI is only predicting words. There is real danger in Anthropic and other AI companies talking about AI like it is thinking, as people treat AI results as rational and logical, when they are not. We should not have people committing suicide because of interactions with word predicting machines. Shame on all the decision makers at AI companies with their careless "move fast and break things" approach to things that have such negative impacts on humanity.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I come from two streams of thought on AI consciousness.  I've been reading science fiction since 1953.  I'm also a retired programmer.  I first read Asimov's "I Robot" when I was in grade school.  I grew up on the Three Laws.    While I've never worked with AI, I know a bit about the way it works and a fair amount about how computers work at the lowest level.  On one hand, the SF side leads me to believe that AI can be managed.  On the computing side, I'm not sure.  There must be rules that govern every decision that software makes.  Because AI is what they call "self-modifying code" there has to be an unbreachable wall around the rules.  I'm sitting on the sidelines biting my nails.

comments.name: AFW
comments.body: There is a point at which a simulation of something becomes practically indistinguishable.  A good example is a movie.  It's doesn't actually move — it is but a simulation of motion, made from 24 still images per second.  But it looks like it's moving, and we talk about it like it's moving, and universally collectively accept that as a "moving picture".  Intelligence is the same way — a point will be crossed where it technically doesn't matter anymore.

comments.name: David Sheppard
comments.body:
With all the anthropomorphisms these people use to describe their AI, you start to wonder if they understand even the first thing about where humans came from. First of all, we evolved through physics and chemistry, each particle of which goes down to the zero-point field and has a deep connection to everything around it, one that was dictated by physics and chemistry and not the forced function of some person's intention. 

The other thing is that practically everything in existence works off contention. Gravity pulls matter in, matter pushes back, and this forms a planet, a surface and an atmosphere where life and humanity evolved. Even many species and humans have two halves that work in contention, opposable thumbs, arms, and two halves of the brain with different perspectives connected and presided over by the executive function of a corpus callosum. All part of a process called "function follows form", where the thing works the way chemistry and physics allow it to work. These AI engineers are using the process "form follows function," where they force matter to do their bidding. In no way made the function of a human being. 

Therefore, creators are the bad actors here and not the code they generate. They should be held accountable in a court of law same as all those who do harm to others intentionally or not, should the warnings of harm to humanity actually come to pass. They are turning an auto loose on the streets and just shouting at it to control its movement.

comments.name: sc
comments.body:
The question of whether AI is conscious (or, in some sense, alive) is a subtle one which is ultimately very relevant.  But we can say much without directly taking it, and its difficulties, up.

Basically, current AI models are developed to produce human-like responses.  It is not just that this is some goal for our convenience, it is that the programs work by analyzing vast amounts of human-created data (books, movies, articles,...) and producing results which fit in with those.  Even when we ask them to solve a problem, they do it not by direct logical reasoning but by looking for patterns in what humans have already done, to emulate.

What has become apparent is that this means they will copy human faults as well:   they will violate their directives, they will lie, they will conceal their misdeeds.  (And they are immensely powerful hackers.)  

All this we understand *now*, without answering questions of whether they are conscious or think in a creative sense, and all of these imply swift action -- some sort of regulation -- is necessary.

comments.name: RM
comments.body:
Emotion, introspection--really? On the way to humaness? There's a lot more to humaness than that.

I've read nothing about moral reasoning, systems of ethics, values. And then there's all the human conditions of sensory input, all of them and how they integrate. Vision and hearing are the easy ones. Touch, taste, and smell: not so easy. And how about learning from our--think personal--mistakes, particularly in relationships--think personal.

AI-speak seems to be solely focused on cognitive rationality as the metric of performance. Introspection? Prove this is more than logical regress, a well defined philosophy concept. Emotion? How can that be "defined" in purely rational constructs?

The claim of killing off humanity in a decade is an entirely different issue. Just how is that supposed to happen?

In somewhere safe like your enclosed backyard, they should be free to be by themselves, but at the park where there’s other children, adults, and who knows what else, your children should be supervised at all times. Nowadays people have to beware of kidnapping and trafficking issues. Ultimately, if you asked me the question, “do children need more supervision — or less?”I'd say that children need both free reign and independence, and supervision and protection. I grew up in a relatively safe neighborhood, and we knew many of our neighbors and as a homeschooler I have a lot of free time on my hands. So, walking down the street to play with the neighbor kid was perfectly safe. There are many neighborhoods where it is not safe to let you child play alone, and it is sometimes hard to know what is safe and what is not, but in order for a child to develop into an independent adult they need to be independent as a child too. It would be unfair to judge today's parents and say they don't let their child be independent enough, or that they are letting their child do too much alone. comments.name: Addy
comments.body: In the article, “Are We Overprotective of Children?” Jeremy Engle discusses a debate about how protective people should be of their kids. I understand both the concerns about children’s safety and the concern that they will not develop independence properly. Dr. Gray points out that “more than a dozen studies draw an association between overprotective parenting and increased rates of anxiety and depression in children”. I personally wish I had a little more freedom when I was younger for this reason, I think I became paranoid of danger because of how protective my parents were of me. Conversely, some people would argue that being paranoid is better than being careless, especially for children. In my opinion, some parents are far too overprotective with their children, and it ends up doing more harm than good for that child in the future. Dr. Gray continues by saying how parents “assume they’re fragile and it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy,”. Giving kids more freedom would lead to more confidence and less anxiety, but ultimately a child’s safety is what is most important. Maybe trusting kids to keep themselves safe by a certain age is the best way to go.

comments.name: Khir

The article says that kids need chances to take reasonable risks and solve problems by themselves instead of having adults rescue them from every mistake. comments.name: Charles Truett
comments.body: Trump has made public discussions of climate change so ideological that practical steps to adapt to it have been displaced by proclamations of beliefs.  Climate change is demonstrably no hoax because it has happened repeatedly in human history since Roman times. The current warming cycle began about 1850 when the Little Ice Age petered out.  A scientific study conducted in 2005 by Mosberg et alia ( https://www.nature.com/articles/nature03265) showed that the atmospheric warming that took place until 1990 was similar to that which occured during the Medieval Warming Period (ca. 950-1250 ).  Global warming is therefore not, in contrast to what climate ideologues claim, primarily caused by humans or even industrialization.  As can been chemically proved however, we can amplify it by burning plants or hydrocarbons.  At the time of the Medieval Warming Period, the were less than 1  billion humans, now there are  8.  The Medieval Warming Period was a major factor in the demise of classic Mayan civilization and the Norse settlements on Greenland.  This warming period, even if it ends after 300 years like the last one, can damage human civilization much more by then.  Practical adaption and a careful eye of the stability of the North Atlantic current should be the order of day in the meantime.  Alas, Trump prioritizes wooing voters in Pennsylvania's last coal mining region in order to hold this key swing state.  India and Indonesia pander to their miners and farmers.

What I don't understand is why John cares enough to stick around, risk his mega-deal with the U.S. military, & see that Hal receives a proper burial. Was it all a cover for trying to get back the ring & using it to...do what? Become a rival lantern to Guy Gardner?

I also don't get why Hal went to prison. He was trying to eliminate a very powerful alien, albeit one who was a benefactor to the community.  And if he and Stewart hadn't done something about the Manhunter, then the other group of aliens were going to blow up the town. So what crime was Jordan guilty of? 

Despite these questions, I love this series. And I love how James Gunn is connecting pieces of the DC universe, similar to how the MCU did it, spanning 20+ movies. The Justice League of America comic books did that back in the day, counting Superman, Batman, Flash, Wonder Woman, Green Arrow and Lantern, & others as members.

Still a lot to be revealed, I think, including whether this is a one-off or if there will be a Lanterns season 2. If it does continue, they have to figure out a way to include Kyle Chandler; he's just too good not to be a part of it.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I was in a vocational metallurgy program at a local community college in the late '70s.  One of my instructors was a metallurgist who did a lot of work as an expert witness in materials related law suits.  He believed very strongly that there ought to be some kind of technical court for things like this.  It was a Two Cultures thing where judges and lawyers came from a liberal arts background and were ignorant of things like the mechanical properties of steel.  Politicians have the same problem with computing.  In the broadest sense, it's easy to see that AI development is going too fast because it's a finance bubble.  AI is also getting overhyped in an effort to feed the bubble.  The rest of us are being forced to be beta testers.  There are lots of unforeseen consequences of AI waiting to be revealed.  It's going to be like the Industrial Revolution.  The cultural and economic effects will be huge.  We need to do a better job of managing the change.  That includes a combination of technical knowledge and ethics.  I wish there were an easy fix.  I read a quote yesterday that fits this situation very well.  It was to the effect that for every complex problem there is a simple solution and it's wrong.
